Refrigerated whole blood preserved the Lumipulse ratio for 24 hours

Refrigerated whole blood preserved the Lumipulse ratio for 24 hours

In 20 participants, the FDA-cleared Lumipulse p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio remained within prespecified stability criteria after refrigerated whole blood was held for 24 hours; 48 hours showed 9.8% mean absolute error and proportional bias.

Key quantitative results: The cohort included 20 participants (mean age 76.5 years; 70% female), including seven with cognitive impairment and 13 cognitively healthy individuals.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Aβ42Preanalytics

Added October 24, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70517; PMID:42908786; PMCID:PMC13683560

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The practical result is strongest at 24 hours, not 48. Refrigerated K2-EDTA whole blood produced nearly identical ratios after 24 hours and met prespecified regression and error criteria. At 48 hours the average absolute error approached 10% and proportional bias appeared, so the extension is a possible workflow option rather than a new universal handling standard.

Study design

Twenty people provided three K2-EDTA tubes. One was processed within two hours, while paired tubes were held at 4°C for approximately 24 and 48 hours before centrifugation and same-day Lumipulse analysis. Stability was evaluated by ordinary least squares regression, error index, Bland-Altman analysis, and Deming regression.

Key quantitative results

  • The cohort included 20 participants (mean age 76.5 years; 70% female), including seven with cognitive impairment and 13 cognitively healthy individuals.
  • Correlation with the two-hour condition was R=0.998 at both 24 and 48 hours, and both delayed conditions met prespecified regression and error-index criteria.
  • Mean absolute percentage error for the ratio was 5.6% at 24 hours and 9.8% at 48 hours.
  • Deming regression found no constant bias, but proportional bias emerged at 48 hours; the individual p-tau217 and Aβ42 analytes showed no bias through 48 hours.

What changed

The study supplies paired operational evidence that a hub-and-spoke laboratory can potentially accept refrigerated whole blood the next day without on-site centrifugation.

Strength of evidence

Moderate analytical-implementation evidence because each participant served as their own control and prespecified stability methods were used. Confidence is limited by the 20-person single-site sample, one tube type, one platform, controlled refrigeration, and absence of clinical classification endpoints.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A validated local workflow could expand specimen access for clinics without centrifuges, but laboratories should not generalize the 24- or 48-hour findings beyond the studied conditions or override manufacturer instructions without verification.

Field medical relevance

Useful for questions about preanalytics, rural access, courier timing, ratio stability, sample rejection, and why an analytically acceptable transport condition is distinct from diagnostic clinical utility.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study used the Version 2 FDA-cleared Lumipulse plasma kits and directly tests whether the ratio can tolerate transport from sites without centrifugation. It does not amend the cleared instructions for use or validate other assays, tubes, temperatures, or shipping conditions.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Next-day refrigerated transport could reduce dependence on on-site centrifugation and ultra-low-temperature storage, but actual laboratory acceptance, courier policy, cost, and reimbursement remain local decisions.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can every laboratory hold specimens for 48 hours?
No. The 48-hour condition showed proportional bias and nearly 10% mean absolute error, and the result is limited to one controlled K2-EDTA/Lumipulse workflow.
Did delayed processing change diagnostic classifications?
The study assessed analytical stability, not clinical decision agreement or patient outcomes.
Does this change the FDA-cleared labeling?
No. It is supplemental implementation evidence, not a regulatory labeling change.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Twenty participants at one center
  • K2-EDTA and 4°C conditions only
  • No real-world shipping stress test
  • No clinical classification or outcome analysis
  • 48-hour proportional bias
  • Assay-specific findings
